Name: affect_labeling_debiasing

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) an LLM can benefit from affect labeling as a debiasing intervention, (2) the effect is opposite to existing emotion-steering work because it reduces emotion's influence rather than amplifying/injecting it, (3) the effect is selective to affect-biased judgments versus length-matched controls/reappraisal, and (4) the mechanism is mediated by a deflatable affect representation. This is a genuinely new regulatory framing and causal test relative to prior emotion steering / emotion-circuit work. The setting is not brand-new, but the question is meaningfully different enough to be novel if executed carefully. The delta from closest prior work is concrete: from probing/steering emotion representations to testing whether explicit emotion naming suppresses their downstream causal impact on reasoning.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether naming emotion in LLM inputs reduces affect-driven judgment errors. If true, it matters to interpretability, emotion/safety research, and any downstream system exposed to emotionally framed inputs, especially triage or decision support. The strongest one-line case: affect labeling could become a simple, general debiasing prompt for emotion-laden inputs. Uptake is plausible because it is actionable and easy to test; even a null result would be informative for whether human affect-labeling transfers to LLMs. That said, the practical reach is somewhat bounded because the effect may be niche, model-specific, or small, and the proposal does not yet establish broad application value beyond a few framed tasks.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is testable but still somewhat underspecified. Main gaps: 'affect-driven errors' and 'affect representation' are broad; mediation via probing plus activation steering can easily overstate causal interpretation; and the proposal risks confounding labeling with added deliberation, extra tokens, or instruction-following. The experiment plan is decent and mostly feasible, but it needs stronger controls, clearer task construction, and better identification of the mechanism. Related work is positioned well enough, but the mechanistic claim will be hard to defend without more rigorous causal tests. If the effect is real and robust, this could be a serious venue paper; as written, it needs tighter scope and stronger falsifiability.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_teaching

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims are: (1) LLM explanations exhibit a curse-of-knowledge effect measured by downstream learner gains, (2) teaching quality worsens as teacher topic competence rises, and (3) an internal learner-knowledge representation can be located and causally steered to improve teaching. The behavioral question is crowded in recent LLM teaching/tutoring and ToM work, so the novelty is mostly in the specific curse-of-knowledge framing plus the mechanistic causal-intervention angle, not in the general task. The closest prior family is LLM pedagogical steering / simulated-learner teaching / mentalizing-in-teaching; the delta is moving from prompt-level adaptation to probing and intervening on an internal learner model, with a downstream learning-gain metric.
revision_notes: State explicitly what is new relative to EducationQ, PEARL, and 'Do LLMs Mentalize When They Teach?' by naming the exact behavioral gap and why existing metrics cannot test it.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is whether LLMs give audience-agnostic, expert-biased explanations that harm learner gains, and whether this can be fixed by modeling the learner. Who cares: tutoring-system builders, education researchers, interpretability/ToM researchers, and safety-critical education contexts like patient instruction. If true, serious practitioners would likely change how they prompt, evaluate, and instrument LLM tutors, because the result directly ties explanation style to downstream learning outcomes. The strongest one-line case is: if LLMs systematically teach worse as they know more, then current 'better model = better tutor' assumptions are unsafe and misleading.

Name: strategic_vagueness_escape_hatch

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that must be novel: (1) answer-content semantic specificity, not confidence wording or abstention, is a difficulty-gated behavioral axis; (2) models use reduced specificity as a self-protective strategy when anticipated error risk is high; (3) vague answers can mask recoverable correct knowledge, operationalized as a Knowledge-Masking Gap; (4) there exists a locatable, steerable commitment/specificity direction distinct from verbal uncertainty features; (5) suppressing that direction recovers hidden correct answers without merely increasing recklessness. Relative to the cited landscape and search summary, this is a real delta from VUF/calibration, ambiguity detection, and abstention work. The strongest novelty is the answer-content-specificity framing plus the masking-gap operationalization and VUF dissociation. The main limitation is that it is adjacent to the recent 'knowing but not showing' family and steering/probing work, so some pieces may read as a natural extension unless the dissociation is made airtight.
revision_notes: State the 3-5 core novelty claims explicitly in the intro as claim/findings/mechanism/setting, not just in broad framing.
Sharpen the contrast table against VUF, abstention, ambiguity-detection, and 'knowing but not showing' papers with one-row deltas: output variable, mechanism, observable, intervention target.
Define precisely where novelty lives: behavioral finding (difficulty-gated specificity), measurement (Knowledge-Masking Gap), and mechanism (separable commitment direction).
Add at least one setting where answer-content specificity is uniquely consequential and not reducible to abstention/confidence, to strengthen the 'meaningfully different setting' case.
Pre-register failure conditions under which the work would collapse into existing uncertainty/calibration results, to show the claim is non-trivial rather than relabeling hedging.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is strategic underspecification of answer content that hides usable knowledge. Stakeholders include calibration/hallucination researchers, honesty and safety evaluators, and deployers in high-stakes advice settings where vague non-answers can be harmful. If true, the result could shift evaluation from confidence labels and abstention toward semantic specificity and hidden-knowledge recovery, which is meaningful. The strongest case is that models may already know the correct specific guidance yet default to vague content as an error-avoidance policy. However, the proposal's application reach is not yet fully demonstrated: it only includes a small high-stakes instance, and it remains unclear whether practitioners would materially change deployment policies absent stronger evidence that this happens frequently and harms outcomes. The 'so what' test is passed for parts of the safety/evals community, but less clearly for broader ML unless prevalence and downstream consequence are shown.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete and testable, with explicit experiments, controls, and thresholds, but several technical gaps remain. The central construct 'anticipated error-risk' is underspecified: how it is measured without leakage or circularity is critical. 'Specificity' is also vulnerable to confounding with answer length, style, politeness, and task format. The Knowledge-Masking Gap is promising but forced commitment can create guessing, and hidden-state probes can overstate recoverable knowledge unless trained/evaluated very carefully. The mechanistic claim of a distinct commitment direction separable from VUF is ambitious and currently under-justified; cosine and AUROC alone may not establish causal distinctness. The clinical/legal component is too underspecified for serious claims. Overall, this could become a solid ML paper if executed well, but it needs tighter definitions, stronger controls, and clearer experimental design to support the mechanistic and strategic language.

Name: polarity_load_tracking

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that would need to be novel: (1) performance degrades as a function of the number of simultaneously active negations, not just sentence-level negation presence; (2) negation is represented as a separable additive polarity flag attached to otherwise positive content; (3) a distinctive behavioral signature distinguishes this from generic difficulty, especially double-negation being easier than same-count independent negations and dominance of polarity-drop errors; (4) the polarity signal is locatable, decodable, and causally manipulable via patching/steering; (5) this matters in multi-step reasoning and a clinical decision setting. Relative to prior work, the broad intuition that negation increases reasoning/working-memory load is already substantially occupied by recent benchmarking and memory-bias papers, so the proposal cannot claim that framing as novel. The real delta is the specific parameterization by simultaneous active negation count, the additive-flag hypothesis with nontrivial behavioral signatures, the named polarity-drop failure mode, and especially the full location-plus-causal-intervention account. That is nontrivial and more specific than an obvious next step, but still somewhat adjacent to existing probing/WM and negation work rather than a wholly new problem or task.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is failure to preserve negated facts through multi-step reasoning, leading to silent polarity reversals. People who would care include reasoning-robustness researchers, interpretability researchers, and safety/application domains like clinical NLP where negated findings can flip decisions. The strongest case is that silent negation loss is a compact, safety-relevant failure mode that may expose a broader memory-like bottleneck in LLM reasoning. If the result holds, follow-up work could build benchmarks, mitigation methods, and mechanistic analyses around polarity tracking; if it fails, that also constrains a popular working-memory-style explanation. This is more than a niche curiosity, but it is still somewhat specialized unless the proposal better demonstrates prevalence in practical settings and broader generalization beyond crafted reasoning chains. It could influence how researchers diagnose reasoning failures, though probably not shift the whole field unless the causal evidence is especially strong and general.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete and testable, with explicit hypotheses, controls, thresholds, and causal experiments. The core hypothesis is falsifiable, and the proposed controls for length/depth/surface form are thoughtful. However, there are important technical risks and some overreach. The 'separable additive polarity flag' claim is stronger than what the proposed evidence may actually establish; decodability plus patching does not by itself prove additive representation rather than correlated latent state. The double-negation comparison is promising but may still admit alternative explanations such as training frequency or logical simplification effects. The causal story needs sharper specification: where patching vectors come from, how they are identified independently of answer content, and how mediation is computed robustly. The proposal also relies heavily on bespoke thresholds (e.g., >=4pp, >=6pp, AUROC>=0.80) that read as arbitrary and could become success-criterion gaming rather than principled inference. Related work is directionally adequate but currently under-specific given the crowded nearby space. If executed well, this could be a solid mechanistic reasoning paper for a serious ML venue, but only if the claims are narrowed and the experimental logic is tightened to rule out generic difficulty/confidence confounds and probe leakage.

Name: acquisition_prerequisite_gating

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) the observed LM acquisition timeline can be reframed as a causal prerequisite graph rather than a descriptive order; (2) surgical single-capability training-data ablation can selectively delay one capability while preserving downstream signal; (3) prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity, dose-response, and rescue can identify true gating edges; (4) per-edge gating strengths can be assembled into a sparse empirical skill tree stricter than temporal order. Relative to the search summary, this is meaningfully novel: prior work is largely descriptive about when capabilities emerge, or causal only for isolated constructions/curriculum effects. The closest prior family is developmental-order/emergence studies plus narrow causal-intervention work on specific constructions and curriculum learning. The actual delta is the move from temporal emergence to cross-capability causal dependency mapping. This is non-trivial, though it is adjacent to obvious next-step intervention work and depends heavily on whether the ablations really isolate capabilities.

This is an important and reusable question, and even a null result would matter by arguing the timeline is not a skill tree. Likely uptake is moderate to strong in interpretability and language acquisition circles, with some downstream relevance to curriculum and dataset design. However, real-world application impact is somewhat indirect unless the proposal demonstrates actionable changes to training practice or scaling behavior beyond small models.

Name: endogenous_filler_buffer

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) spontaneous natural-language filler in free generation is an adaptive self-allocated compute buffer, not merely stylistic noise; (2) filler placement follows a just-in-time allocation law, rising before locally hard reasoning steps; (3) endogenous filler is load-bearing in a way dissociable from length/content-matched substantive text or neutral padding; (4) a locatable internal buffer-request signal predicts and causally governs filler placement; (5) this signal can drive a buffer-gated efficiency controller. Relative to prior work, the crowded part is only the broad idea that filler/pause tokens can support hidden computation. The actual delta—endogenous rather than experimenter-injected filler, adaptive allocation law, and a steerable internal request signal—is meaningfully distinct and non-obvious. The closest prior family is injected filler/pause-token computation and hidden-computation decoding work; the proposal's delta is shifting from exogenous compute tokens to self-emitted natural-language filler as an adaptive resource. Novelty is strong but not maximal because much of the mechanism rests on extending an existing filler-computation story into a new behavioral setting rather than introducing a wholly new theory.
